name: Industry Use Cases
blurb: What AI is actually used for, industry by industry, with ROI, vendors, risks, and case studies.

metrics.source: US Census Bureau, Business Trends and Outlook Survey (national estimates)

questions.text: In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

During the next six months, do you think this business will be using Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

sectors.name: Accounting
sectors.blurb: Transaction classification, audit anomaly detection, close automation, and the shift from sampling to full-population testing, with AICPA, IMA, and benchmark sources.

sectors.name: Agriculture
sectors.blurb: Vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, and autonomous equipment at commercial scale, tracked through USDA ERS, FAO, satellite data providers, and the equipment and standards bodies.

sectors.name: Banking
sectors.blurb: Fraud detection and credit models are decades old. Generative AI in service and compliance is the new frontier, under Fed SR 11-7 model risk supervision.

sectors.name: Churches and Faith Organisations
sectors.blurb: Sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations, from Barna research and faith-tech platforms to Notre Dame ethics work.

sectors.name: Construction
sectors.blurb: Computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning, sourced from AGC, BuiltWorlds, and the proptech and contech trackers.

sectors.name: Defense
sectors.blurb: Decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing as programs of record. DIU as the commercial on-ramp. Free federal procurement data first, subscription analysts labeled.

sectors.name: Education
sectors.blurb: Tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy from K-12 through university, with market tracking and this site's own course catalog.

sectors.name: Energy
sectors.blurb: Grid optimisation, exploration, and the datacenter power crunch that makes energy both an AI user and AI's binding constraint, from EPRI and DOE to the utilities and oilfield majors.

sectors.name: Government
sectors.blurb: Federal AI use inventories, GAO oversight, international readiness indexes, and the state legislatures writing AI law tracked on this site.

sectors.name: Healthcare
sectors.blurb: Imaging diagnostics, clinical documentation, and drug discovery, with the health-specific model benchmarks and KLAS and Rock Health tracking adoption.

sectors.name: Hospitality
sectors.blurb: Revenue management, service automation, and AI assistants as a booking discovery channel hotels now compete in, from Skift and AHLA to the distribution and restaurant tech vendors.

sectors.name: Insurance
sectors.blurb: Underwriting, claims triage, and fraud detection under active regulator supervision, with NAIC, AM Best, and the Evident insurance index.

sectors.name: Legal
sectors.blurb: Research, review, and drafting at scale, the citation-sanction lesson, and the benchmarks and trade bodies that measure legal AI accuracy.

sectors.name: Manufacturing
sectors.blurb: Predictive maintenance, machine vision on the line, and generative design, with A3 automation data, IoT Analytics, and NIST standards work.

sectors.name: Media
sectors.blurb: Generation tools transformed production while training-data litigation transformed the business relationship with AI; cross-linked to the lawsuit tracker.

sectors.name: Mining
sectors.blurb: Autonomous haulage and ore-body modelling in the sector that automated early, from USGS exploration data and Earth MRI to Rio Tinto, Komatsu, KoBold, and the AI-native explorers.

sectors.name: Nonprofits
sectors.blurb: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets, with governance capacity as the constraint, from CEP and NTEN to Candid and the equity project.

sectors.name: Real Estate
sectors.blurb: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest AI and now federally regulated under FHFA and CFPB quality-control rules; plus valuation, leasing, and property-management platforms with methodology disclosed.

sectors.name: Retail
sectors.blurb: Demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation at volume, with NRF, Coresight, and IHL tracking the deployments.

sectors.name: Sports
sectors.blurb: Performance analytics, broadcast automation, and officiating assistance, from NCAA and NFHS governance to Hudl, Catapult, and the sports technology research network.

sectors.name: Transportation
sectors.blurb: Autonomous driving is the visible front; AI also runs freight matching, maritime navigation, transit, and aviation, from IMO and EASA to the trucking, shipping, and aviation majors.

analysis.body:
Current AI adoption among US businesses has grown substantially since measurement began in late 2024. As of the most recent period, 23.2% of businesses report using AI in their operations, up from 17.3% in the initial measurement period. The trajectory shows consistent upward movement, with adoption climbing from the high teens through the low twenties over the measured timeframe.

Businesses report significantly higher expectations for AI adoption over the next six months compared to current usage. The latest forward-looking figure stands at 27.3%, indicating that roughly 4 percentage points more businesses expect to adopt AI than currently use it. This gap between current usage and near-term expectations suggests active consideration and planning for AI implementation across the business sector, with momentum building toward expanded adoption.

The share of businesses that do not know their AI status remains relatively stable and substantial. In the most recent period, 9.6% of respondents answered "do not know" to the current usage question, while 25.8% selected "do not know" for the six-month outlook. The larger uncertainty around future AI use compared to current status suggests that many businesses have not yet formulated definite plans, even as the industry appears to be in a phase of rapid expansion. Meanwhile, 67.2% of businesses currently report not using AI, though this proportion has declined from 71.6% at the survey's start.

findings.body: The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey asks a representative sample of US firms every two weeks whether they used AI in the last two weeks - the closest thing the industry has to an official adoption statistic, shown live above. What the cross-sector reading adds: adoption is wildly uneven. The sectors on this site with the deepest sourced coverage - real estate, agriculture, mining, transportation - are not the sectors with the loudest AI marketing, and the sectors with the loudest marketing are not the heaviest measured users. Sector bodies that count deployments (A3 for robotics orders, NRF and Coresight for retail, AHLA for hotels, EPRI for utilities) consistently report deployment concentrated in a minority of large firms while the median firm is still piloting.
findings.heading: Adoption is measured, and the measurement disagrees with the hype in both directions

findings.body: Banking has supervised models since the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 guidance in 2011; insurance regulators coordinate through the NAIC's model bulletin; and automated valuation models in real estate came under federal quality-control rules from FHFA and CFPB in 2024-2025, effective before most sectors had any AI rule at all. The pattern across the 21 sectors: where a prudential regulator already existed, AI arrived into a supervision framework, and the compliance conversation is about model risk management, not about whether rules apply. Where no such regulator exists, the governing pressure comes from the state legislatures tracked in this site's law database instead.
findings.heading: The regulated industries got AI rules before the AI boom

findings.body: Mining has run driverless haul trucks in production since the early 2010s - Rio Tinto's autonomous fleet is the canonical case - and agriculture ships vision-guided sprayers and autonomous tractors as commercial products from the major equipment makers, not as pilots. Maritime autonomy has an IMO regulatory code in development and aviation has an EASA AI roadmap. The finding that generalizes: autonomy matured fastest where the operating environment is bounded (a mine site, a field, a shipping lane) and slowest where it is open (city streets), which is why the robotaxi story and the autonomous-haulage story read a decade apart.
findings.heading: The physical industries automated earliest and quietest

findings.body: Healthcare has HealthBench for clinical answers; legal and accounting have the vals.ai evaluations built with the professions' own bodies; banking and insurance have the Evident indexes ranking named institutions on AI maturity. General model leaderboards tell a hospital or a bank nothing about their liability; the sector benchmark movement exists because the question that matters is no longer "which model is smartest" but "which system is safe for this regulated task", and every sector page here links its own measurement bodies.
findings.heading: Benchmarks are going sector-specific, because general benchmarks stopped answering the buyer's question

findings.body: Utilities use AI for grid optimization and demand forecasting (EPRI and DOE grid-modernization programs anchor that work), while at the same time datacenter load growth has made electricity the limiting input for the AI industry itself - the capex telemetry on this site tracks the same buildout from the spending side. No other sector sits on both sides of the ledger, and the interaction runs in both directions: AI demand is reshaping utility planning, and utility interconnection queues are reshaping where AI capacity gets built.
findings.heading: Energy appears twice: as an adopter and as the binding constraint

findings.body: The media sector's AI relationship is being negotiated in court: the training-data lawsuits tracked live in this site's lawsuit database are simultaneously licensing negotiations, and the settlements and rulings coming out of them are writing the de facto rules for how creative work enters training corpora. Media is thin on this page by design - two sourced points - because the substantive record is the docket, and it is cross-linked rather than duplicated.
findings.heading: In media, litigation is the industry structure

findings.body: Federal agencies publish AI use-case inventories, GAO audits them, and international indexes (Oxford Insights, OECD.AI, the Stanford AI Index) rank national readiness - while the same governments write the rules everyone above must follow, including the 2,400+ state bills in this site's law tracker. The three roles pull in different directions, and the tension is visible in the sources: the strongest federal accountability source, GAO's consolidated AI inventory, sits behind a bot wall this site declines to fake.
findings.heading: Government is adopter, referee, and scorekeeper at once

findings.body: Every one of the 153 sector points links a verified primary source: government and statistical programs first, then trade associations and standards bodies, then the operating companies' own published programs. Paywalled analyst estimates (Gartner, IDC, McKinsey), equity-fund marketing pages, and vendor vertical brochures are excluded on principle; sources that block automated verification (IEA, GAO's inventory, USDA's main site) are named as walled rather than quietly substituted. Where a number appears on a sector page, the page it came from still serves it.
findings.heading: What this coverage will not do

synthesis.body:
As of early 2026, business use of AI has reached 23.2% across the economy according to the Census Bureau's latest biweekly measurement, up from 17.3% roughly a year prior. This represents a sustained acceleration in adoption that masks significant variation by sector and application type. The Census data, collected continuously since late 2023, provide the only consistent cross-sector measurement of AI use, asking firms whether they activated AI in their business functions during the preceding two weeks. Adoption ranges from 5.3% in mining to 43.5% in information services, with finance and professional services at 36.5% and 43.3% respectively, while hospitality remains at 8.5% and transportation at 7.9%, indicating that AI deployment follows capital intensity and data-availability patterns rather than spreading evenly across the economy.

The applications driving adoption cluster around three core workflows: anomaly detection and risk assessment in finance and insurance, automation of document and data processing in professional services and legal practice, and optimization of operations through computer vision and predictive analytics in manufacturing, retail, and transportation. In accounting, the shift from statistical sampling to population-level testing through vendors like MindBridge represents a structural change in how firms conduct audits, enabled by machine learning applied to entire transaction ledgers. In healthcare, diagnostic imaging and clinical documentation support steady adoption at 24.7%, anchored by publicly funded research through the NIH and evaluated against clinical benchmarks like HealthBench, which tests model responses against 5,000 physician-curated conversations. In agriculture, Climate FieldView's prescription services show measured yield improvement of 5 bushels per acre for farmers using seed scripts, demonstrating ROI at the operational layer, while investment capital concentrated on companies with real unit economics rather than speculative positioning, with global agrifoodtech funding at $16.2 billion in 2025, down 3% but filtered toward sustainable business models. Across these domains, vendors emphasize explainability and human oversight rather than full automation, reflecting both regulatory requirements and organizational risk tolerance.

The vendor landscape shows concentration in high-stakes domains and fragmentation in commodity functions. Financial AI vendors like MindBridge, agricultural platforms like Climate FieldView, legal-tech firms like LexisNexis and EvenUp, healthcare systems benchmarked through HealthBench and KLAS Research, and retail intelligence providers like Retailgrid and IHL Group have shipped working systems with measurable operational impact. Concurrently, large language models available on public registries show wide performance variance on specialized tasks: Vals AI's benchmarks document that leading models achieve 65.71% accuracy on financial reasoning but drop to 34.29% on legal analysis, with search-tool selection materially affecting performance across models. This variance explains why sector-specific implementation over generic AI appears to drive ROI in practice. Defense procurement, tracked through SAM.gov and the Defense Innovation Unit, reveals a government-to-vendor pipeline where adoption is documented through contracts rather than self-report, with roughly 200 active AI use cases out of 1,200 planned across 23 federal agencies as of the GAO's most recent inventory, indicating that government AI remains heavily in pilot and planning phases.

Regulatory frameworks are crystallizing sector by sector rather than emerging as unified federal rules. The Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk management guidance from 2011 now governs how banks deploy AI in credit and AML decisions, imposing compliance costs that factor into deployment ROI. The NAIC has surveyed insurers on AI governance and risk controls, emphasizing that human judgment remains essential and that insurers remain legally responsible for outcomes regardless of algorithmic decision-making. The CFPB and FHFA jointly finalized quality control standards for automated valuation models in real estate, requiring random testing and conflict-of-interest controls on mortgage-collateral AI—the first binding federal rule on any AI system in the real estate sector. The FAO and international working groups on e-Agriculture engage in dialogue on digital innovation but without published compliance frameworks for agricultural AI. The EU AI Act requires transparency marking for synthetic media, the Copyright Office is writing policy on training-data rights and copyrightability of AI-generated content, and the International Maritime Organization's MASS Code sets goal-based autonomy rules for shipping even as no cargo vessels currently operate autonomously in international trade. This fragmentation means organizations deploying AI must navigate sector-specific compliance rather than applying a single national standard, and must anticipate that rules will continue to evolve as government agencies process scale and risk.

Return on investment evidence concentrates in domains where AI reduces manual labor or improves decision quality on measurable outcomes. Climate FieldView's 5 bu/ac yield improvement, Dr. Squatch's 31.89% recommendation click-through rate and $32,978 attributed revenue, Samsara's 380,000+ accidents prevented through dashcam AI, and Building Engines' promise of NOI improvement through property operations automation all present concrete value propositions. However, most sources do not disclose costs of implementation, integration timelines, failure rates, or how returns scale across firm sizes. Manufacturing's 23.4% adoption and growing interest in autonomous operations are documented without published case studies of throughput or safety gains. The Legal sector's 43.3% adoption rate masks unresolved questions about whether document-review automation genuinely improves outcomes or simply shifts junior-lawyer skill development into simulation and redesign.
